Magnetic safety factor $q$ (or $q$-profile) quantifying the pitch of magnetic field lines on a flux surface. The safety factor is fundamental for MHD stability analysis and determines the rational surfaces where instabilities can occur.

$$q = \frac{1}{2\pi} \oint \frac{B_{\phi}}{B_p R} dl_p$$

where $B_{\phi}$ is [toroidal_magnetic_field](#toroidal_magnetic_field), $B_p$ is [poloidal_magnetic_field](#poloidal_magnetic_field), $R$ is major radius, and $dl_p$ is the differential poloidal arc length.

Physical significance:

The safety factor determines MHD stability limits through the Kruskal-Shafranov criterion. Rational surfaces where $q = m/n$ (integer $m$, $n$) are resonant for MHD modes. Lower $q$ values indicate higher [plasma_current](#plasma_current) and reduced stability margins. The minimum safety factor $q_{\text{min}}$ and edge safety factor $q_{95}$ are key operational parameters. See [plasma_current](#plasma_current) and [magnetic_field](#magnetic_field) for field structure relationships.

Measurement methods:

Safety factor profiles are determined from equilibrium reconstruction using external magnetic measurements. The $q$-profile relates to [plasma_current_density](#plasma_current_density) through $\nabla \times \mathbf{B} = \mu_0 \mathbf{J}$ and can be inferred from [flux_loop_voltage](#flux_loop_voltage) measurements. MSE (motional Stark effect) diagnostics provide direct $q$-profile measurements in some devices.

Typical values:

On-axis: $q_0 = 0.7$-1.5, edge: $q_{95} = 3$-6 for stable operation. Operation below $q_{\text{min}} < 1$ leads to sawtooth oscillations. H-mode operation typically requires $q_{95} > 2.5$ for stability.

Sign convention: Positive when toroidal current and toroidal field are in same direction, following右手螺旋定则 for standard tokamak operation.

Electron kinetic temperature $T_e$ representing the mean thermal energy per electron. In fusion plasmas, electron temperature typically ranges from tens of eV in the edge region to several keV in the plasma core.

Thermodynamic relation:

Electron temperature relates to [electron_pressure](#electron_pressure) via the ideal gas law:

$$p_e = n_e k_B T_e$$

where $n_e$ is [electron_density](#electron_density) in m$^{-3}$, $k_B = 1.381 \times 10^{-23}$ J/K is Boltzmann's constant, $T_e$ is in K, giving $p_e$ in Pa. When using $T_e$ in eV, apply conversion: $p_e = n_e T_e \times 1.602 \times 10^{-19}$ Pa.

Physical significance:

Temperature determines [energy_confinement_time](#energy_confinement_time) and fusion reactivity. Higher electron temperatures improve confinement quality and increase fusion reaction rates. The temperature gradient drives [electron_heat_flux](#electron_heat_flux) and affects [plasma_resistivity](#plasma_resistivity). See also [ion_temperature](#ion_temperature) and [electron_temperature_at_magnetic_axis](#electron_temperature_at_magnetic_axis).

Measurement methods:

Thomson scattering provides local [electron_density](#electron_density) and temperature measurements. Electron cyclotron emission measures temperature from radiation spectrum. X-ray spectroscopy determines temperature from continuum and line emissions. Interferometry provides line-integrated density for pressure calculations.

Typical values:

Edge region: 10-200 eV, core region: 1-20 keV in high-performance tokamak plasmas. On-axis values in [electron_temperature_at_magnetic_axis](#electron_temperature_at_magnetic_axis) typically reach 5-15 keV during auxiliary heating.

Electron number density $n_e$ representing the volumetric concentration of electrons (thermal plus non-thermal) in the plasma. In fusion plasmas, electron density typically ranges from $10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$ in the edge region to $10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ in the plasma core. Electron density determines plasma conductivity and affects [plasma_resistivity](#plasma_resistivity).

Thermodynamic relation:

Electron density relates to [electron_pressure](#electron_pressure) and [electron_temperature](#electron_temperature) via the ideal gas law:

$$p_e = n_e k_B T_e$$

where $p_e$ is electron pressure in Pa, $k_B = 1.381 \times 10^{-23}$ J/K is Boltzmann's constant, and $T_e$ is in K. When using $T_e$ in eV, apply conversion: $p_e = n_e T_e \times 1.602 \times 10^{-19}$ Pa.

Physical significance:

Electron density determines plasma conductivity through $\sigma = n_e e^2 \tau / m_e$ and affects [plasma_current](#plasma_current) requirements. Higher density improves confinement through increased collisionality but may reduce [energy_confinement_time](#energy_confinement_time). Density gradients drive [electron_heat_flux](#electron_heat_flux) and affect [plasma_current_density](#plasma_current_density) profiles. See [plasma_density_at_magnetic_axis](#plasma_density_at_magnetic_axis) for core values.

Measurement methods:

Interferometry measures line-integrated electron density through phase shift of laser beams. Reflectometry determines density profiles from microwave reflection. Thomson scattering provides local density measurements with high spatial resolution. Interferometry systems use multiple chords for 2D reconstruction. Density measurements are essential for [electron_pressure](#electron_pressure) calculations and equilibrium reconstruction.

Typical values:

Edge region: $10^{18}$-$10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$, core region: $10^{19}$-$10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ in high-performance tokamak plasmas. On-axis values in [plasma_density_at_magnetic_axis](#plasma_density_at_magnetic_axis) typically reach $5 \times 10^{19}$ - $2 \times 10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ during high-performance operation.

Sign convention: Positive density indicates particle concentration, following standard plasma physics conventions.

Poloidal magnetic field vector $\mathbf{B}_p$ lying in the poloidal plane (R-Z plane), comprising radial and vertical components. The poloidal field is generated by toroidal [plasma_current](#plasma_current) and external poloidal field coils, providing the rotational transform necessary for tokamak confinement.

$$\mathbf{B}_p = B_R \hat{e}_R + B_Z \hat{e}_Z$$

where $B_R$ is [radial_magnetic_field](#radial_magnetic_field), $B_Z$ is [vertical_magnetic_field](#vertical_magnetic_field), both in T.

Physical significance:

The poloidal field is generated by toroidal [plasma_current](#plasma_current) and external poloidal field coils. It provides the rotational transform of field lines necessary for tokamak confinement and determines plasma shape through equilibrium force balance. Poloidal field strength affects [safety_factor](#safety_factor) profiles and MHD stability limits. See [poloidal_magnetic_field](#poloidal_magnetic_field) for magnitude relationships and [magnetic_field](#magnetic_field) for total field structure.

Relation to plasma current:

The poloidal field relates to [plasma_current_density](#plasma_current_density) via Ampère's law:

$$\nabla \times \mathbf{B}_p = \mu_0 j_{\phi} \hat{e}_{\phi}$$

where $j_{\phi}$ is toroidal current density in A/m$^2$ and $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ H/m.

Measurement methods:

Poloidal magnetic field is measured using magnetic probes and flux loops positioned around the plasma. [Flux_loop_voltage](#flux_loop_voltage) integration provides field change information. Equilibrium reconstruction codes invert external magnetic measurements to determine internal field structure. MSE diagnostics provide direct poloidal field measurements in some devices. Vector field analysis requires multiple measurement locations.

Typical values:

Poloidal field strength typically ranges from 0.1-1 T, much smaller than toroidal field but essential for confinement. Field strength varies with radius and [plasma_current](#plasma_current).

Sign convention: Positive poloidal field follows the right-hand rule for toroidal current direction, consistent with [plasma_current](#plasma_current) measurements and standard tokamak conventions.

Poloidal magnetic flux $\Psi$ threading a surface in the poloidal plane, defined as the integral of [poloidal_magnetic_field](#poloidal_magnetic_field) through a surface:

$$\Psi = \int \mathbf{B}_p \cdot d\mathbf{A}$$

where $\mathbf{B}_p$ is poloidal magnetic field in T and $d\mathbf{A}$ is the differential area element in m$^2$.

Physical context:

Poloidal flux is a fundamental coordinate for describing tokamak equilibria. Flux surfaces are contours of constant $\Psi$, and the normalized poloidal flux $\Psi_N = (\Psi - \Psi_{\text{axis}}) / (\Psi_{\text{LCFS}} - \Psi_{\text{axis}})$ is used to label flux surfaces from magnetic axis ($\Psi_N = 0$) to [plasma_boundary](#plasma_boundary) ($\Psi_N = 1$).

Measurement:

Poloidal flux changes are measured by [flux_loop_voltage](#flux_loop_voltage) via Faraday's law: $V = -d\Psi/dt$.

Sign convention: Positive when surface normal points upward (positive Z direction).

Minor radius evaluated at the [plasma_boundary](#plasma_boundary) (last closed flux surface), calculated as half the difference between outboard and inboard major radii at the midplane. Minor radius defines the characteristic size scale for normalized radial coordinates and plasma cross-sectional area.

$$a_{\text{boundary}} = \frac{R_{\text{out}} - R_{\text{in}}}{2}$$

where $R_{\text{out}}$ is [radial_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary](#radial_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary) at outboard midplane and $R_{\text{in}}$ is the radial coordinate at the inboard midplane, both in m.

Physical significance:

This quantity defines the radial extent of confined plasma and is used in calculating plasma cross-sectional area, [plasma_volume](#plasma_volume), and shape parameters. It serves as the characteristic length scale for normalized radial coordinates. Minor radius affects [energy_confinement_time](#energy_confinement_time) through scaling laws and determines [plasma_current](#plasma_current) requirements. See [radial_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary](#radial_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary) for aspect ratio and [elongation_of_plasma_boundary](#elongation_of_plasma_boundary) for shape relationships.

Relation to shape parameters:

Together with [elongation_of_plasma_boundary](#elongation_of_plasma_boundary) $\kappa$, determines the plasma cross-sectional area: $A_p \approx \pi a^2 \kappa$. This relationship is fundamental for plasma volume and surface area calculations.

Measurement methods:

Minor radius is determined from equilibrium reconstruction using external [magnetic_field](#magnetic_field) measurements. [Flux_loop_voltage](#flux_loop_voltage) integration provides boundary geometry information. Plasma imaging systems measure boundary coordinates directly. Minor radius analysis requires [magnetic_axis](#magnetic_axis) location and [plasma_boundary](#plasma_boundary) identification. Geometric calculations use standard tokamak coordinate systems.

Typical values:

Small tokamaks: 0.2-0.5 m, medium tokamaks: 0.5-1.0 m, ITER: ~2 m. Minor radius scales with machine size and determines plasma cross-sectional area.

Sign convention: Positive minor radius measured from magnetic axis to boundary, following standard tokamak geometry conventions.

Electron heat flux vector $\mathbf{q}_e$ representing the thermal energy transported by electrons. In cylindrical coordinates, components include radial [radial_electron_heat_flux](#radial_electron_heat_flux), poloidal, and toroidal directions. Electron heat flux is a primary energy loss channel in tokamak plasmas and determines [energy_confinement_time](#energy_confinement_time) through transport processes.

Transport relation:

Heat flux relates to temperature gradient and thermal diffusivity:

$$\mathbf{q}_e = -n_e \chi_e \nabla T_e$$

where $n_e$ is [electron_density](#electron_density) in m$^{-3}$, $\chi_e$ is [electron_thermal_diffusivity](#electron_thermal_diffusivity) in m$^2$/s, $\nabla T_e$ is [electron_temperature](#electron_temperature) gradient in eV/m.

Physical significance:

Electron heat flux is driven by temperature gradients and turbulent transport, determining energy confinement quality. Understanding and controlling heat flux profiles is essential for achieving good [energy_confinement_time](#energy_confinement_time) and predicting plasma performance. Heat flux affects [plasma_current](#plasma_current) requirements and [safety_factor](#safety_factor) limits. See [electron_thermal_diffusivity](#electron_thermal_diffusivity) for transport coefficients and [radial_electron_heat_flux](#radial_electron_heat_flux) for radial transport.

Measurement methods:

Electron heat flux is inferred from [electron_temperature](#electron_temperature) and [electron_density](#electron_density) profile measurements using transport analysis. Thomson scattering provides local temperature and density measurements for gradient calculations. Electron cyclotron emission measures temperature profiles. Heat flux analysis requires equilibrium reconstruction using [magnetic_field](#magnetic_field) measurements and [plasma_current](#plasma_current) data.

Typical values:

Core region: $10^4$-$10^6$ W/m$^2$, edge region: $10^6$-$10^8$ W/m$^2$ near the pedestal. Heat flux typically increases toward the edge due to steeper temperature gradients and reduced confinement.

Sign convention: Positive heat flux indicates energy flow in the direction of decreasing temperature, following the direction of $\nabla T_e$.
